breakfast.name: Lakh (Millet Porridge with Yogurt)
instructions: Steam millet couscous
Mix with yogurt, sugar, butter
Serve warm or cold

breakfast.name: Bread with Zrig
instructions: Mix yogurt with water and sugar
Serve with bread for dipping
breakfast.description: Bread with diluted sweetened yogurt drink.

breakfast.name: Harissa (Wheat Porridge — Mauritanian Style)
instructions: Soak cracked wheat briefly
Simmer in water until completely soft and porridge-like
Stir frequently — the wheat absorbs water and thickens
Add generous butter — Mauritanian cooking is historically very generous with fat
The butter is the flavor component
Season with salt
Optional sweet version: add milk and sugar
Mauritanian harissa (not the North African chili paste — completely different word-use)
A warming, sustaining porridge for cold desert mornings
The Sahara's temperature swings: very hot by day, cold at night — the hot porridge is for dawn
Desert nomads historically ate this porridge before moving with their herds
breakfast.description: Mauritania's wheat porridge — cracked wheat simmered until soft and generously buttered. Despite sharing a name with North African chili paste, this is entirely different: a filling, fatty porridge for cold desert dawns. Mauritanian cooking is historically generous with fat (reflecting pastoral wealth — camel butter, sheep butter), and this porridge demonstrates it.

breakfast.name: Dates with Camel Milk
ingredients: Camel milk (fresh — or dried/powdered camel milk)
instructions: Mauritania has one of the world's largest camel populations — camel milk is the traditional dairy
Camel milk is more nutritious than cow milk — higher in vitamins C and B, lower in fat
The flavor is slightly saltier and thinner than cow milk — unique
Drink camel milk cold alongside dates — this is the Mauritanian/Saharan morning
The date-milk combination provides complete nutrition: sugar, fat, protein, vitamins
In the Mauritanian nomadic tradition, this is the complete meal
Dates grow throughout the Mauritanian oases
The Sahara nomad's breakfast: the camel provides milk; the palm provides dates; the desert provides both
Mauritania's camel milk production is among the world's highest — now being commercialized
The sweet date against the slightly salty camel milk is a flavor contrast of the desert
breakfast.description: Mauritania's desert morning — fresh dates alongside cold camel milk. Mauritania has one of the world's largest camel populations; camel milk is the traditional dairy, slightly saltier and more nutritious than cow milk. The date-camel milk combination provides complete nomadic breakfast nutrition: date sugars + milk fat and protein. The Sahara's complete meal.

lunch.name: Thieboudienne (Fish and Rice)
instructions: Stuff fish with herb paste, fry
Make tomato-onion sauce
Add vegetables and fish
Cook vegetables, remove
Add rice to cook in broth
Serve rice topped with fish and vegetables
lunch.description: Fish and rice in tomato sauce — Mauritanian version.

lunch.name: Méchoui (Whole Roast Lamb)
instructions: Clean lamb, rub inside and out with butter, salt, cumin, garlic
Roast over coals or in large oven
Turn occasionally for even cooking
Cook 4 hours until meat falls off bone
Tear pieces by hand
lunch.description: Whole roast lamb — the Mauritanian feast centerpiece.

lunch.name: Thieboudienne (Senegalese Rice-Fish Borrowed)
ingredients: Stuffing: parsley, garlic, chili, dried fish (guedj), oil
instructions: Note: thieboudienne is the national dish of Senegal — but due to shared Wolof-influenced coastal culture
Mauritania's Atlantic coast Wolof communities eat thieboudienne
The dish is described fully in the Senegal file — this entry notes the cross-cultural borrowing
Fish-stuffed with the spiced herb paste, fried then braised in tomato with broken rice
The broken rice absorbs the fish broth and becomes extraordinarily flavorful
The Atlantic coast of Mauritania and Senegal is culturally and culinarily connected
The dish traveled with Wolof fishing communities who settled along both coasts
lunch.description: Mauritania's Atlantic coast fish rice — shared from Senegalese Wolof fishing communities who settled the Mauritanian coast. Thiéboudienne (broken rice with fish stuffed with a spiced herb paste, braised in tomato broth) crosses the Mauritania-Senegal border with the fishing communities. Cultural food exchange across political borders.

lunch.name: Couscous de Chameau (Camel Couscous)
ingredients: Camel meat (tougher cuts need long braising — shoulder, neck)
instructions: Camel is Mauritania's prestige meat — served at celebrations, for honored guests
Camel meat is lean and has a slightly gamey, sweet flavor — similar to beef but drier
The tougher cuts require very long braising — 2-3 hours
Braise camel with spices, onion, tomato in water
The broth will be rich and slightly sweet from the camel fat
Steam couscous three times over the broth (the traditional couscoussier method)
Assemble: couscous mounded, camel placed on top, broth ladled over
Smen (aged Mauritanian camel butter) dotted on top
Camel couscous is the greatest Mauritanian hospitality dish
A guest receives camel; a regular family meal would use lamb or goat
lunch.description: Mauritania's prestige hospitality dish — camel (Mauritania's honor meat) braised for hours until tender, served over triple-steamed couscous with the richly flavored broth. Camel is reserved for honored guests and celebrations. Mauritanian aged camel butter (smen) is spooned over the assembled dish, adding an intensely funky depth.

dinner.name: Couscous bil Lahm (Couscous with Lamb)
instructions: Steam couscous
Make lamb stew with vegetables
Mound couscous, ladle stew over
dinner.description: Couscous with lamb and vegetable stew.

dinner.name: Grilled Camel Meat
instructions: Cut camel meat into steaks
Marinate with onion, garlic, cumin
Grill over charcoal
Serve with rice
dinner.description: Grilled camel meat — a desert tradition.

dinner.name: Méchoui bil Camel (Whole Roasted Camel)
ingredients: Whole camel (or camel leg for smaller gatherings)
instructions: Méchoui of camel is served at Mauritanian state events, major weddings, and Eid
A whole camel feeds 50-100 people
Marinate with spices, garlic, camel fat
Traditionally slow-roasted in a pit over embers — hours of cooking
Modern: very low oven, 8-12 hours for a whole camel
The camel fat renders and bastes the meat from inside
The meat is lean outside the fat deposits — but the connective tissue enriches the braising
The whole camel is a symbol of wealth and generosity
Mauritania is one of the few countries that regularly serves whole roasted camel
The camel's hump (almost pure fat) is the most prized piece for honored guests
dinner.description: Mauritania's ultimate feast — whole roasted camel, the most extravagant hospitality gesture in Mauritanian culture, feeding 50-100 people. Marinated and slow-roasted for 8-12 hours until the connective tissue breaks down and the meat is tender. The hump (nearly pure fat) goes to the most honored guest. One of the few countries in the world where whole camel roasting is regularly practiced.

dinner.name: Asida (Stiff Millet Porridge)
instructions: Asida is the Mauritanian staple — a thick, stiff millet porridge
Boil water with salt
Add millet flour gradually while stirring — no lumps
Cook 15-20 minutes, stirring vigorously — the porridge becomes very stiff
Turn out onto a flat plate — it holds a dome shape
Top with melted butter or camel fat
Eat by tearing pieces with the right hand and dipping into the accompanying sauce
Asida is the everyday starchy base — like Malian tô, Nigerian tuwo, or Ugandan ugali
The Sahel's universal stiff porridge — called different names but the same technique
Mauritania's nomadic tradition: asida was portable, made from dried millet that traveled with the herds
dinner.description: Mauritania's stiff millet porridge — the Sahel's universal starchy base (called tô in Mali, ugali in Kenya, sadza in Zimbabwe), eaten by tearing pieces with the right hand and dipping into sauce. Millet flour cooked until stiff enough to hold a dome shape. The nomadic tradition kept dried millet as a portable staple carried with the camel herds.

dinner.name: Thiou Bou Yapp (Meat Rice)
instructions: This is the Mauritanian meat rice — similar to West African thiébou
Brown meat with onion in oil
Add tomato, spices
Add rice — stir to coat in the oil and spices
Add water — enough to cook the rice
Cover and cook until rice is done and has absorbed the broth
The meat flavor permeates the rice entirely
The bottom of the pot often forms a crust (slightly burnt rice) — this is cherished, not wasted
Thiou bou yapp is Mauritania's everyday dinner in coastal and urban areas
The rice-meat one-pot is the most efficient use of ingredients and fuel
The crust (sokhna in Wolof) is scraped and distributed as a treat
dinner.description: Mauritania's meat rice — lamb braised then cooked together with rice in the same pot, the meat flavor permeating each grain. The crusted bottom (sokhna) scraped from the pot is the cherished prize. A one-pot meal that conserves both fuel and water — practical for the desert. Coastal Mauritanian urban families eat this daily.

snacks.name: Dates and Camel Milk
instructions: Serve fresh dates with a glass of camel milk
snacks.description: The traditional Saharan snack — dates with fresh camel milk.

snacks.name: Açai (Dates Stuffed with Peanut Paste)
ingredients: Large dates (Medjool or local Mauritanian variety)
instructions: Remove pit from dates — the medjool variety opens cleanly
Fill the cavity with peanut paste — press in generously
The sweetness of the date against the savory-salty peanut
Optional: use ground almond or walnut paste instead
The stuffed date is the Saharan/Mauritanian party nibble
Dates are the Mauritanian snack as ubiquitous as chips elsewhere
Every tea ceremony, every gathering, dates are present
The peanut-stuffed variety is a step up from the plain date
No cooking required — the desert provides the ingredients
snacks.description: Mauritania's stuffed date — large sweet dates filled with peanut paste, the sweetness of the date against the savory-salty peanut creating the Saharan snack pair. No cooking. Dates are ubiquitous at every Mauritanian gathering and tea ceremony; the peanut-stuffed version is the elevated form.

snacks.name: Zrig (Camel Milk Laban)
ingredients: Optional: sugar or salt depending on preference
instructions: Zrig is Mauritania's fermented camel milk drink — the Sahelian equivalent of yogurt or kefir
Fresh camel milk left in a skin bag (historically) or vessel ferments naturally in Sahara heat
The result is mildly sour, slightly thick, refreshing
Can be drunk thick (yogurt consistency) or diluted with water
Some prefer salty; some prefer sweet
Zrig is Mauritania's national drink — offered to every guest before water or tea
To refuse zrig is a social misstep
The fermentation creates natural probiotics — the Sahelian health drink
Nomads sustained long journeys on zrig alone — it provides water, protein, and probiotics
The slightly sour camel milk is more refreshing than sweet milk in heat
snacks.description: Mauritania's national drink — fermented camel milk (zrig), mildly sour and naturally probiotic, offered to every guest before water or tea. Refusing zrig is a social misstep. Nomads sustained desert crossings on zrig alone: it provides hydration, protein, and probiotics. The Sahelian equivalent of yogurt-as-drink, made from the camel rather than the goat or cow.

snacks.name: Camel Cheese (Fromage de Chameau)
instructions: Camel milk cheese is notoriously difficult — camel milk's proteins behave differently from cow milk
The proteins form curds less readily — more acid or rennet is needed
Heat camel milk to 65°C — not boiling
Add rennet or lemon juice
Curds will form but more slowly and less firmly than with cow milk
Drain gently through cloth
The result is a soft, slightly salty fresh cheese
Camel cheese has been a food science challenge — fully stable hard camel cheese was only developed commercially in the 21st century
Mauritanian traditional fresh camel cheese is soft and consumed quickly
The slight saltiness and the unique camel milk flavor are the characteristics
snacks.description: Mauritania's difficult fresh cheese — camel milk barely curdled into a soft, salty fresh cheese. Camel milk proteins resist curdling (a food science challenge that commercial producers only solved in the 21st century); traditional Mauritanian camel cheese is soft and consumed immediately. The subtle, slightly salty camel milk flavor is unlike any cow or sheep cheese.

desserts.name: Thiakry (Millet and Cream)
instructions: Steam millet couscous
Mix with condensed milk, cream, vanilla
Add raisins
Serve chilled
desserts.description: Sweet millet couscous in rich cream.

desserts.name: Tagella (Sand-Baked Bread)
instructions: Tagella is the Tuareg and Mauritanian nomadic bread — baked under hot sand and embers
Mix flour, water, salt into a thick dough
Shape into a flat disc
Rake hot embers aside, bury the dough disc in hot sand directly under the embers
Cover with more hot embers and sand
The sand conducts heat evenly around the bread
After 15-20 minutes, dig out and brush off the sand
The exterior is dark — brush it fully
The inside is cooked and soft
The sand-baked bread tradition is thousands of years old
It requires no equipment — just desert sand and fire
The slightly smoky, earthy flavor comes from the sand-ember contact
desserts.description: Mauritania's nomadic sand bread — dough disc buried under hot desert embers and sand, baked by the sand's thermal conductivity. The oldest bread baking technique: no pan, no oven, just fire and sand. The slightly smoky, earthy exterior and soft inside is the result of perfect even heat from surrounding sand. Thousands of years old.

desserts.name: Lakh (Millet-Soured Milk Dessert)
instructions: Steam fine millet couscous briefly
Mix while warm with soured milk or yogurt and sugar
The warm millet soaks up the cold soured milk
The contrast of warm grain and cold fermented milk is the temperature pleasure
Add groundnut paste for richness if desired
Lakh is Mauritania's / Senegal's sweet millet dessert
Shared across the Sahel — same concept under different regional names
The fermented milk provides tang; the millet provides substance; the sugar provides sweetness
A complete, nutritious dessert from only regional ingredients
Eaten after the main meal as a cooling, filling end to the dinner
desserts.description: Mauritania's millet dessert — steamed fine millet couscous mixed with soured milk and sugar, the warm grain soaking up the cold fermented milk. The temperature contrast (warm millet, cold soured milk) is the experience. Shared across the Sahel from Mauritania to Senegal under different names. Complete nutrition from regional ingredients only.

drinks.name: Atay (Mint Tea)
instructions: Brew strong green tea
Add mint and generous sugar
Pour back and forth to foam
Serve three rounds, each sweeter
drinks.description: Mauritanian mint tea ceremony — three rounds of sweet tea.

drinks.name: Zrig (Yogurt Drink)
instructions: Mix yogurt with water and sugar
Serve cold

drinks.name: Thé à la Menthe (Three-Glass Tea Ceremony)
ingredients: Fresh mint (or dried in desert areas)
instructions: The three-glass Mauritanian tea ceremony is similar to Moroccan atay
But in Mauritania it's more elaborate and takes more time
First glass: strong, very bitter — 'bitter as death'
Second glass: slightly sweetened — 'sweet as life'
Third glass: very sweet, mint-forward — 'sweet as love'
Each glass is poured from height to create foam
The ceremony takes 30-45 minutes — this is intentional
The time is for conversation, business, and connection
Refusing tea in Mauritania is the most significant social insult
The three-glass ceremony is the framework for all Mauritanian social interaction
Nomads carried tea, mint, and sugar on long desert crossings — the ceremony travels with the people
drinks.description: Mauritania's supreme social ritual — three glasses of green tea with mint and sugar, each progressively sweeter (bitter as death, sweet as life, sweet as love), poured from height to create foam, taking 30-45 minutes. Refusing is the most significant social insult. The ceremony is the framework for all Mauritanian social interaction — business, hospitality, and friendship happen over these three glasses.
